                                            EmbodiedSplat: Personalized Real-to-Sim-to-Real Navigation with Gaussian
                                                                 Splats from a Mobile Device

                                                           Gunjan Chhablani1 *, Xiaomeng Ye2 , Muhammad Zubair Irshad3 , Zsolt Kira4
                                                                        1,2,4
                                                                              Georgia Tech, 3 Toyota Research Institute
                                                 {1 chhablani.gunjan, 3 muhammadzubairirshad}@gmail.com, {2 xye87, 4 zkira}@gatech.edu




arXiv:2509.17430v2 [cs.CV] 23 Sep 2025
                                                                     Abstract

                                         The field of Embodied AI predominantly relies on simula-
                                         tion for training and evaluation, often using either fully syn-
                                         thetic environments that lack photorealism or high-fidelity
                                         real-world reconstructions captured with expensive hard-
                                         ware. As a result, sim-to-real transfer remains a major
                                         challenge. In this paper, we introduce EmbodiedSplat,
                                         a novel approach that personalizes policy training by ef-
                                         ficiently capturing the deployment environment and fine-
                                         tuning policies within the reconstructed scenes. Our method
                                         leverages 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) and the Habitat-Sim
                                         simulator to bridge the gap between realistic scene cap-
                                         ture and effective training environments. Using iPhone-
                                         captured deployment scenes, we reconstruct meshes via GS,
                                         enabling training in settings that closely approximate real-
                                         world conditions. We conduct a comprehensive analysis
                                         of training strategies, pre-training datasets, and mesh re-       Figure 1. Overview of EmbodiedSplat: Mobile phone captures
                                         construction techniques, evaluating their impact on sim-          are used to generate reconstructed meshes via 3D Gaussian Splat-
                                         to-real predictivity in real-world scenarios. Experimen-          ting (GS). Agents are trained within these reconstructed environ-
                                         tal results demonstrate that agents fine-tuned with Embod-        ments in simulation before being deployed in the real world, en-
                                         iedSplat outperform both zero-shot baselines pre-trained          abling effective sim-to-real transfer. Our analysis demonstrates
                                         on large-scale real-world datasets (HM3D) and syntheti-           a strong sim-to-real correlation across both types of generated
                                         cally generated datasets (HSSD), achieving absolute suc-          meshes, highlighting their ability to bridge the gap between simu-
                                                                                                           lation and real-world performance.
                                         cess rate improvements of 20% and 40% on real-world Im-
                                         age Navigation task. Moreover, our approach yields a high
                                         sim-vs-real correlation (0.87–0.97) for the reconstructed
                                         meshes, underscoring its effectiveness in adapting policies       key bottleneck is the sim-to-real gap, where handcrafted or
                                         to diverse environments with minimal effort. Project page:        synthetic simulation environments (e.g. HSSD [25]) strug-
                                         https://gchhablani.github.io/embodied-splat.                      gle to capture the complexity and variability of real-world
                                                                                                           settings, necessitating the use of real-world reconstructions
                                                                                                           for effective policy training. On the other hand, real-world

Figure 2. The EmbodiedSplat Pipeline: Pipeline for integration of real-world captures with Habitat-Sim [39] and subsequent deployment.
The first stage (a.) involves capturing the scene using Polycam [38] and Nerfstudio [48] which produces RGB frames, associated iPhone
GT depth maps, and poses. In the second stage (b.), we use DN-Splatter [49] to train GS using depth and normal regularization, with
normals from Metric3D-V2 [16] monocular encoder. A mesh (.ply) is created using Poisson reconstruction from the GS. In the third
stage (c.), the mesh is processed and loaded into Habitat-Sim [39] for training the agent in simulation. In the last stage (d.), the policy is
deployed in the real-world in the same scene for image-goal navigation.

Captured and MuSHRoom Scenes: For scenes with DN
meshes and P OLYCAM meshes, we select only the largest
navmesh island within each scene. We ensure that the
largest island covers most, if not all, of the navigable areas
in the scene. This step is crucial due to the relatively smaller
sizes of these scenes compared to HM3D scenes. Hence,
we generate only 1000 training episodes and 100 evalua-
tion episodes per scene. By selecting the largest navmesh
island, we minimize the risk of incorrectly treating entities
other than the floor as navigable.
Evaluation Metric: We consider Success Rate (SR), the
fraction of successful episodes out of all the episodes, as           Figure 4. Zero-shot val. SR for HM3D pre-trained policy.

cies. An episode is considered successful if the agent stops           Fig. 4 presents the results of the zero-shot evaluation

of steps (1000 for simulation, 100 for real) are over.              Performance varies significantly based on scene size, com-

                                                                   In this experiment, we investigate the necessity of pre-

                                                                   and validation data are derived from ImageNav episode
                                                                   generation, as described in Sec. 3.3. To ensure diversity,
                                                                   start-goal locations for training and evaluation episodes are
                                                                   randomly sampled. The best validation success rates for all
                                                                   policies on their respective scenes are presented in Fig. 9.

The zero-shot HM3D policy achieves a 50% success rate,
demonstrating our hypothesized lack of generalization.
This is in contrast with the results reported in Silwal et al.
[46] showing 90% zero-shot success rate in the real-world.
We attribute this discrepancy to the structural and semantic
differences between the lounge and the apartment-style
scenes typically encountered in HM3D. Fine-tuning on the
P OLYCAM and DN mesh reconstructions of this scene im-

5.3. Does continuous training on large-scale                          In this work, we introduced a comprehensive pipeline for
     datasets improve zero-shot performance?                          bridging the gap between real-world and simulated envi-
                                                                      ronments in training embodied agents using 3D Gaussian
                                                                      Splats (GS) and Polycam. By leveraging the MuSHRoom
                                                                      dataset and custom iPhone-captured scenes, we demon-
                                                                      strated an efficient and scalable approach to policy personal-
                                                                      ization, leveraging 3D scene reconstruction from low-effort
                                                                      collects, enabling high-quality training for the ImageNav
                                                                      task. Our pipeline facilitates accessible and replicable scene
                                                                      collection without requiring specialized hardware or signif-
                                                                      icant costs, making it a practical solution for large-scale
                                                                      embodied AI research. We evaluated overfitted, zero-shot,
                                                                      and fine-tuned policies, showing that fine-tuning pre-trained
                                                                      policies on real-world scene reconstructions improves sim-
Figure 11. Average zero-shot success rates on respective vali-        to-real transfer. We also analyzed the differences between
dation sets over different stages of pre-training on HM3D.            GS-generated DN meshes and P OLYCAM meshes, finding
                                                                      that P OLYCAM more closely resemble real-world scenes.
   Fig. 11 presents average zero-shot success rates across                This work lays the foundation for seamlessly integrat-
HM3D validation set, P OLYCAM meshes, and DN meshes                   ing real-world scene captures into simulation, expanding
at various stages of HM3D policy pre-training. This                   the applicability of embodied AI systems. Another promis-
analysis aims to determine whether continuous perfor-                 ing avenue is integrating GS directly into training, replacing
mance improvements on HM3D validation scenes translate                visual observations and goal images to enhance learning ef-
to improved zero-shot performance on our Captured                     ficiency. Furthermore, we aim to extend the use of Gaussian
scenes. We observe that while performance initially in-               Splats to more complex embodied AI tasks, such as rear-
creases, it begins to deteriorate or plateau at approximately         rangement and mobile manipulation, broadening its impact
400M steps, despite continued improvements on HM3D                    across diverse real-world applications.

A. Real-world Deployment on Stretch Robot




                                                                            Figure 14. Hello Robot Stretch in lounge scene


Figure 13. Framework for real-world evaluation on a Stretch robot.


   Since the stretch robot is not equipped with GPUs, we
develop a framework for deploying a policy on a remote
cluster, and performing inference using POST requests
from the robot. An overview of this arrangement is shown
in Fig. 13. Specifically, we create a Flask server that runs
on a remote compute node, port-forwarded to an Ubuntu
20.04 machine with ROS noetic installed. The same ma-
chine is connected to a Stretch robot via ethernet connec-
tion. We use the home-robot [43] repository as frame-
work to convert discretized actions from the policy into con-                Figure 15. Goal images used in lounge scene
tinuous space using the “StretchNavigationClient”. A script
running on the machine consumes the ROS topics for image
observations from the robot, and passes this along with the          B. Generating ImageNav episodes
goal image to the policy and receives the next action based
on these observations.                                               To generate ImageNav episodes, we build upon Habi-

                                                                on image-goal navigation, out-of-domain generalization,
Fig. 16 and Fig. 17 shows the rendering differences for the     the effects of reconstruction quality and training strategies.

DN meshes have diffused and darker colors, and some holes       neural scene representations for real-world robotic appli-

D. Expanded Related Work
D.1. 3D Scene and Mesh Reconstruction
Recent advancements in 3D scene reconstruction have led
to the development of several notable approaches. Neural
Radiance Fields (NeRF) [35] and subsequent methods [4,
19, 36] have focused on training and improving neural scene
representation techniques. The foundational 3D Gaussian
Splatting (GS) method [24] has inspired a variety of exten-
sions. DN-Splatter [49] improves reconstruction quality by      Figure 18.      Converting the .ply files generated by DN-
incorporating depth and normal regularization with monoc-       Splatter [49] to .glb files using Blender. Transform +Y Up is
                                                                kept unchecked following conventions of Habitat-Sim [39].
ular networks. Gaussian Surfels [12] introduces a technique
for flattening 3D Gaussians into 2D surfels, resulting in en-
                                                                   DN-Splatter [49] gives us Poisson reconstructed meshes
hanced mesh reconstruction. GS2Mesh [51] incorporates
                                                                from the Gaussian Splats in .ply format. In order to load
real-world knowledge through stereo-matching to generate
                                                                these meshes in Habitat-Sim [39], we need to convert these
smoother meshes. SuGaR [15] proposes a fast mesh extrac-
                                                                to .glb format. In order to do so, we import the .ply in
tion method using surface-aligned Gaussian splatting.
                                                                Blender and then export them as .glb files while ensuring
D.2. 3D Scene Representation in Robotics                        that +Y Up transform is unchecked, following the conven-
                                                                tions used in Habitat-Sim.
Several studies have explored the use of neural scene
representations [33, 54] and 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS)         F. Episode Statistics for Generated Datasets on

K. Failure modes for HM3D zero-shot on                                Table 8. Overfitted validation success rates after 20M steps.
   lounge scene in simulation
To assess the role of visual fidelity, we analyze zero-shot
HM3D policy trajectories and identified failure modes in
the lounge scene using both DN and P OLYCAM meshes
(Tab. 7) in simulation. We found significant increase in
“Maximum Steps Reached” failures with the DN mesh, in-
dicating low visual fidelity prevents the policy from match-
ing goal images— a key limitation of the pre-trained policy.

  Termination Reason                      P OLYCAM        DN
  Target Reached (success)                       74        55
  Early Stop (Goal Not Visible)                   3         5
  Early Stop (Goal Visible)                      11        16
  Early Stop (Similar Goal Visible)               4         5
  Maximum Steps Reached                           8        19
